query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multiscale surrogate model that explicitly incorporates descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure (e.g., phase distributions, nanoscale precipitate characteristics, and local elastic constant variations) can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 more rapidly (with roughly one-tenth the computation time) and with comparable accuracy (within ±10% error) relative to traditional full‐scale DFT and finite element simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy synthesized with a deliberately engineered hierarchical heterostructure, featuring a controlled distribution of nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries that affect dislocation mobility and crack propagation.
generation.intervention: Implementing a physics‐informed machine learning surrogate model that uses microstructural descriptors (from imaging and spectroscopy) alongside key computed parameters (such as misfit volumes, elastic constants, and phase fraction data) as input to predict mechanical properties under tensile and fracture testing conditions.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing conducted at room temperature under controlled uniaxial tensile loading and standardized fracture tests; the microstructure is verified by high-resolution microscopy techniques to ensure reproducibility of the hierarchical architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical heterostructure mediates local stress fields and dislocation dynamics, where nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries serve to both reinforce the matrix and deflect crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: By capturing the contributions from solid solution strengthening, heterostructure-induced toughening, and interfacial barrier effects in a reduced-order framework, the surrogate model bypasses the intensive computational demands of traditional DFT/FEM approaches while retaining essential microstructural information.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will provide predictions for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture initiation stress that deviate no more than ±10% from experimental measurements and will require roughly 10% of the computational time of established simulation routines. Additionally, it will accurately predict the nature of crack initiation and propagation pathways consistent with in situ fracture observations.
generation.baseline: Conventional simulations using full-scale DFT combined with finite element methods, which are computationally intensive and may not fully capture the effects of hierarchical microstructural features.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis may not hold if the actual heterostructural features exhibit variability (e.g., due to processing-induced defects, unexpected phase instabilities, or anisotropies) that are outside the input parameter range of the surrogate model or if significant scale-dependent phenomena are neglected by the effective medium approximations.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in precisely quantifying the microstructural descriptors for the hierarchical features and in determining the model’s calibration limits; further experimental data across a broader range of processing conditions will be required to refine the surrogate’s predictive capabilities.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTiVAl10 samples with verified hierarchical heterostructures (confirmed via electron microscopy and diffraction techniques). Use the surrogate model to predict mechanical properties (Young’s modulus, yield strength, fracture initiation stress) under standardized tensile and fracture tests. Then, subject the samples to these mechanical tests under identical conditions, recording stress-strain curves and detailed crack propagation maps via high-speed imaging.
measurements: Young’s modulus from the initial elastic slope of the stress–strain curve
Yield strength determined at a 0.2% offset strain
Fracture initiation stress and crack propagation paths from high-speed imaging and post-mortem fractography
Computational time comparison between the surrogate model and traditional simulations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surrogate model predictions deviate by more than ±15% from the experimental values or if the computation time is reduced by less than a factor of 10 compared to conventional simulation methods, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A typical method of choice for truly predictive calculations of alloy properties is density functional theory (DFT). However, explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is mostly out of reach for available DFT implementations. Although this may become possible with general-purpose interatomic potentials,, a fairly robust description can be obtained by using appropriate models, which have been shown to accurately predict strengthening and ductility. These models combine linear elasticity and microscopic principles, and the only required input parameters are certain material properties. Specifically, apart from basic equilibrium properties, such as the molar volume and elastic constants, the strengthening model requires misfit volumes related to concentration derivatives of the alloy volume, while the ductility model relies on surface and unstable stacking fault (USF) energies computed for specific orientations. Importantly, all of these parameters are accessible through simulations using first-principles methods, yet, such simulations are still challenging for disordered MPEAs.

Upon inspection of the fracture surface generated from in situ SEM microtensile testing (fig. S5), both faceted and dimpled regions are present, corresponding to brittle and ductile failure, respectively. Evidently, plastic deformation of the alloy occurs primarily through the ductile fcc phase, which has the aforementioned hierarchical architecture. Dislocation accumulation/storage is enhanced inside the fcc grains due to the presence of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates, which may result in enhanced strain hardening and improved ductility () relative to other reported HEAs. This proposed mechanism accounts for the appreciable work hardening and failure strain of ~5.2% exhibited by the Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 HEA under tension at room temperature.

The modulus of elasticity is an intrinsic property of materials and a key parameter in the design and development of materials. Thus, for engineering applications it is vital to understand this characteristic with high precision in order to both perform finite element calculations or to define constitutive models. However, the test methods currently used, either for static or dynamic regime, have some accuracy issues []. The tensile test is the main static method used for the calculus of the elastic modulus and involves the calculation of the stress–strain diagram slope on the region where only elastic deformations are present. The main problems associated with measuring accuracy for this method are related to alignment, deformation measurement, and data analysis. For homogeneous and isotropic materials, Young’s modulus may also be obtained from a static bending test []. Another static testing method applicable to thin films is indentation [,]. The compression test is not considered a reliable method for the Young’s modulus as long as machine compliance affects the accuracy of the measurements.
